mentions.quote: the king should make it a source of revenue, for the purpose of preventing deception among respectable people
Property without an heir goes to the king, after setting aside what is for the woman's maintenance and for funeral rites
the decision regarding their established practices rests with them, not with the king
these ten offenses the king must investigate himself
Kings who apply punishment correctly are worshipped even by the gods
a king, a lord of the earth, should always act, being devoted to his duties

entities.description: The king is the central authority figure responsible for administering justice, regulating vice, punishing offenders, and protecting the social order.
entities.justification: The king appears across chapters 79 and 80 as the primary agent of law enforcement, revenue collection, and punishment, making him the most prominent figure in these chapters.

mentions.quote: the property of a learned Brahmin should be given to other learned Brahmins
the desire to kill cows and Brahmins
A Brahmin deserving death or mutilation of a limb should enter solitary confinement
Having given all the wealth collected from fines to Brahmins

entities.description: Brahmins are the priestly class who receive special legal treatment — their heirless property stays within the class, they are protected from killing, and fine-revenues are donated to them.
entities.justification: Brahmins appear repeatedly as a specially protected and legally privileged group with distinct inheritance and punishment rules that differ from other varnas.

mentions.quote: A Shudra who takes up the life of an ascetic and devotes himself to chanting and fire-sacrifices, the king should punish that sinner with death

entities.description: The Shudra is the lowest varna, here specifically prohibited from adopting the ascetic lifestyle and Brahminical practices such as chanting and fire-sacrifices.
entities.justification: The Shudra is named as the subject of a specific capital prohibition against crossing varna boundaries by adopting ascetic religious roles.

mentions.quote: A sonless widow, preserving her husband's bed and remaining under the protection of her elders, being chaste, may enjoy his property until death
When her husband has gone to heaven, a woman is entitled to food and clothing
After her husband's death, the family's guardian-wife shall receive her husband's share. For her lifetime, she has no ownership in matters of gift, mortgage, or sale
A sonless woman who is devoted to vows and fasting, established in celibacy, and always engaged in self-control and charity, goes to heaven

entities.description: The widow is a legally constrained figure who may enjoy her deceased husband's property only under strict conditions of chastity and elder-service but lacks full ownership rights.
entities.justification: Chapter 78 is entirely devoted to the widow's legal position as conditional heir, making her the primary legal subject of that chapter.

mentions.quote: For barbarians, outcastes, rogues, gamblers, and ascetics, the decision regarding their established practices rests with them, not with the king
towards an ascetic, a reprimand
A Shudra who takes up the life of an ascetic
mentions.role: normative reference point for ascetic identity

entities.description: Ascetics are recognized as a legally semi-autonomous group whose internal customs are self-regulated, yet they remain subject to royal authority in the form of verbal reprimand.
entities.justification: Ascetics appear as a distinct social category with special jurisdictional status, set apart from ordinary royal subjects.

mentions.quote: The gaming-house keeper (*sabhika*) should conduct the gambling and should himself give the king's share
The gaming-house keeper should forcibly make the loser pay what is due in that place
the gaming-house keeper is the authority, provided that the keeper is honest

entities.description: The sabhika is the licensed operator of a public gaming establishment who collects revenue for the king, enforces debts, and adjudicates disputes among gamblers.
entities.justification: The gaming-house keeper is assigned a specific regulatory and judicial role in chapter 79's gambling code, making them a distinct institutional figure.

mentions.quote: This is the law for *strīdhana*; thus the partition is arranged
The *strīdhana* received by a woman from her father in the Āsura and other forms of marriage
A righteous king should make a woman pay a fine from her Woman's Property

entities.description: Strīdhana is the legal concept of woman's personal property, inherited or gifted to her, with specific rules of succession depending on marriage type and the presence of heirs.
entities.justification: Strīdhana is the central legal concept governing chapters 77's inheritance rules and reappears in chapter 80 as the asset base for women's fines.

surface_names: Āsura and other forms of marriage

mentions.quote: The *strīdhana* received by a woman from her father in the Āsura and other forms of marriage, in the absence of her offspring, is desired to go to her mother and father
mentions.role: marriage form determining inheritance of strīdhana

entities.description: The Āsura marriage is a recognized but lower form of marriage in which property given to the bride reverts to her parents if she dies without issue.
entities.justification: The Āsura form is cited as a specific legal category that alters the default inheritance trajectory of strīdhana, showing the text's attention to marriage-type taxonomy.

mentions.quote: Of reunited coparceners (*saṃsṛṣṭas*), the reunited are heirs; of separated ones, the separated

entities.description: Saṃsṛṣṭas are coparceners who have re-united their shares after a prior partition, creating a distinct mutual-heirship group separate from those who remain separated.
entities.justification: The term is introduced as a technical legal category determining the line of mutual succession within joint-family property law.

themes.topic: Inheritance hierarchy and women's property rights

mentions.quote: Sisters with their husbands should divide it with their kinsmen. This is the law for *strīdhana*
In the absence of daughters, that inheritance goes to the sons. What was given by her kinsmen goes to her kinsmen
The wife who is not unchaste is the heir to her husband's wealth

themes.justification: Chapters 77 and 78 lay out an intricate, gender-sensitive succession ladder for deceased women's property and for property of sonless men, with chastity and kin-affiliation as determining variables.

themes.topic: Conditionality of widows' property rights on chastity and obedience

mentions.quote: A sonless widow, preserving her husband's bed and remaining under the protection of her elders, being chaste, may enjoy his property until death
She is entitled to enjoy her allotted share if she is devoted to serving her elders. If she does not perform this service, she should be assigned only clothing and a morsel of food
a woman who is addicted to adultery is not entitled to the property

themes.justification: The text makes a widow's economic survival explicitly contingent on sexual purity and filial obedience, linking property rights directly to behavioural compliance.

themes.topic: State regulation and licensing of gambling

mentions.quote: the king should make it a source of revenue, for the purpose of preventing deception among respectable people
The gaming-house keeper (*sabhika*) should conduct the gambling and should himself give the king's share
the gambler, having given the king his prescribed share, may gamble openly; in this way, no fault is incurred

themes.justification: Chapter 79 frames gambling not as an activity to be simply banned but as a vice the king can harness through taxation and licensing to prevent worse abuses.

themes.topic: Gambling as a social vice productive of strife and ruin

mentions.quote: One should not engage in gambling, which increases anger and greed. It is a begetter of wicked men, cruel, and a destroyer of men's wealth
strife certainly arises from gambling, as poison from a serpent's mouth, therefore the king should suppress it in his domain

themes.justification: The text opens chapter 79 with a moralistic framing of gambling as inherently destructive, grounding the subsequent regulatory regime in ethical condemnation.

themes.topic: Varna hierarchy and prohibitions on crossing caste boundaries

mentions.quote: A Shudra who takes up the life of an ascetic and devotes himself to chanting and fire-sacrifices, the king should punish that sinner with death
the destruction of the rules of caste and life-stages, and the disruption of the purity of mixed castes

themes.justification: The text treats caste transgressions as criminal offenses requiring royal intervention, with the most severe penalties reserved for Shudras performing Brahminical religious acts.

themes.topic: Royal duty as the foundation of cosmic and social order

mentions.quote: Kings who apply punishment correctly are worshipped even by the gods
a king, a lord of the earth, should always act, being devoted to his duties. And he should appoint all his servants to work for the welfare of the world
Kings and ministers especially suffer from not punishing sinners and from punishing the submissive

themes.justification: Chapter 80 closes the treatise by elevating correct royal punishment to a cosmological virtue, connecting just kingship to divine approval and universal welfare.

mentions.quote: One deserving death deserves a fine of one hundred gold pieces. For mutilation of a limb, half of that; for banishment, twenty-five
The first fine should be imposed for an initial offense; the middle fine is remembered for a continuing one
For children, the old, the sick, and women, the punishment is not beating or a fine

themes.justification: The text articulates a calibrated system of penalties scaled to the nature of the offense, the social category of the offender, and whether the offense is first or repeated.

themes.topic: King's intelligence network and proactive governance

mentions.quote: the king, having been well-informed of these by his spies, should suppress them himself
Those acts done anonymously, the legal arguments of litigants, the agitation of the subjects, and conspiracy among them

themes.justification: The text implicitly treats royal spying as a legitimate and necessary instrument of governance, presupposing an intelligence apparatus through the phrase 'well-informed by his spies'.

themes.topic: Special legal status of the destitute and enslaved

mentions.quote: Those who are dependent on others, and those who are in a state of slavery, are designated as helpless; their punishment is beating
The destitute should be placed in confinement; one should not apply the death penalty

themes.justification: The text recognises a distinct legal sub-class of economically helpless persons (slaves, the destitute) for whom monetary fines are inapplicable and physical or custodial punishment substitutes.

mentions.quote: Miscellaneous matters include what remains after the previous topics, what has fallen outside its proper legal heading, what is introduced from another authority and is inconsistent
Any rule which follows this procedure is considered a miscellaneous matter

themes.justification: Chapter 80 opens with a self-reflective jurisprudential definition of 'miscellany', treating the category of legal remainder as itself a formal topic requiring definition — an implicit metatextual theme.
